newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus leader cancels trip, Kremlin seeks calm.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader cancels trip, Kremlin seeks calm.

text.p: The president of Belarus, feuding with Moscow over the arrest of a Russian television crew, angrily cancelled a visit to Russia on Friday but the Kremlin played down talk of a rift.
President Alexander Lukashenko called off his trip to the Baltic enclave of Kaliningrad after its governor urged him to delay the visit due to concern over the journalists' arrest.
Lukashenko's spokesman Vasily Dolgolev accused Kremlin liberals opposed to closer integration between the two former Soviet states of being behind the governor's decision.

"As a representative of the president I consider that this is an insult to our state...These actions were hardly the initiative of the governor but were planned by Russian opponents of integration," Dolgolev told reporters in Minsk.

He said Governor Leonid Gorbenko's telegram had arrived only hours before Lukashenko had been due to fly to Kaliningrad, which is sandwiched between Poland, Lithuania and the Baltic Sea and is cut off from the rest of Russia by Belarus.
The Kremlin's press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Gorbenko had acted unilaterally without consulting Moscow.
"This incident shows how damaging the initiatives of regional leaders can be when not agreed with the federal centre," Itar-Tass news agency quoted the spokesman as saying.

Yastrzhembsky, speaking at the Volga river resort of Volzhsky Utyos where President Boris Yeltsin is on vacation, said he did not believe the spat over the ORT television crew would exacerbate relations between Moscow and Minsk.
Tass quoted Yeltsin as saying the row showed Lukashenko, 42, was "young and over-sensitive to criticism". Interfax news agency said Yeltsin had described Lukashenko as too "excitable".

Yeltsin and Lukashenko have already traded harsh words over the arrest of the three ORT journalists on July 26 and the Russian leader has threatened to review the union treaty the two signed in May if they are not released.
Two of them face up to five years in jail after being charged with illegally crossing the Belarus-Lithuanian border.
International human rights groups have also urged their release and have criticised limits on press freedom in Belarus, where a referendum last November gave Lukashenko vast powers.
"The court will decide (the journalists') fate," Dolgolev said on Friday. "This is not a matter for presidents. The border must be inviolable. That is in Russia's interests too."

Even before his arrest ORT correspondent Pavel Sheremet had been accused by the authorities of biased reporting and stripped of his press accreditation -- the second Russian television reporter to be so punished this year.
Lukashenko said on Thursday Sheremet was in the pay of unnamed foreign powers. He also accused Russia's liberal First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais of trying to torpedo integration.

Liberals led by Chubais persuaded Yeltsin to water down the Belarus union treaty earlier this year. Kremlin sources said they feared the lack of market reforms in Belarus could hold Russia back and were concerned at giving Lukashenko a political platform in Russia.
On Friday a court in Minsk passed sentence on 14 journalists detained the day before for taking part in and reporting on a petition in support of the ORT crew.
Some of the reporters escaped with an official reprimand but the others were ordered to pay fines of up to $200. The average monthly salary in Belarus is around $60.
